en: The Section on Formal Acts (Karmavastu). Regarding the Section on Formal Acts, here is the summary verse (uddāna):
In the Kāśis, at Vāsavagrāmaka and Senāñjayavastuka,
as well as in Campā, the Blessed Buddha rejected improper actions.
In the land of Kāśī, in the village of Vāsavagrāmaka, there lived a monk named Senāñjaya.
Because of him, the brahmins and householders of Vāsavagrāmaka performed acts of service toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

Whenever visiting monks came to Vāsavagrāmaka, he would settle them, provide them with all necessary requisites, and once their fatigue from the journey was dispelled, [he would direct them] to those families where alms-food was to be sought.
He sent them there to eat, having appointed them to those [tasks].
Now, a certain *sālohita* (maternal relative) had spent the rains retreat in the village of Vāsava;

when the three months of the rainy season had passed, having finished his robes and completed his robe-making, he took up his bowl and outer robe and set out on a walking tour toward Śrāvastī, proceeding by stages on his journey.
While traveling, he arrived at Śrāvastī.
It was the custom of the group-of-six monks that the gate of the Jeta Grove was never left empty by one or another of them.
Upananda was standing at the gate of the Jeta Grove.
He saw him from afar, with a head shaped like a crane's and long-hanging eyebrows;
he observed,
"Some elderly monk is coming here."
"I must go out to meet him. He went out to meet him and said,
"Welcome, welcome, Elder!"
He said,
"I pay homage to the teacher.
He reflected:
The elder said, "This man does not know his teacher (ācārya), nor does he know his preceptor (upādhyāya). [The other asked:
"Sālohita, from how far have you come?"
From Vāsavagrāma. What is there? A monastery.
Is this a dwelling? Or is it an obstacle? What kind of dwelling is it?
What kind of deficiency is it?
That monastery where there is an abundance of requisites is [an absence of deficiency];
that where there is a lack of requisites is deficiency.
"If that is so, this is the monastery where the monk named Senāñjaya resides.
Because of him, the brahmins and householders of Vāsavagrāma perform services for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;
and from here, visiting monks come there."

Having pacified him and provided him with all necessary requisites, once his fatigue from the journey was dispelled, he sent him to eat at those families where the monks were habitually assigned alms-food.
It was the custom of the group of six (ṣaḍvargika) monks that whenever they heard anything at all, they would gather together at night and report it to one another:
"Nanda and Upananda, how much longer must we endure this hardship?"
"Is there anything among you, or has anyone heard of anything, where there might be a magnificent manifestation?
Upananda replied,
"There is."
In the Kāśis, in the village of Vāsava, there dwells a monk named Senāñjaya.
Having heard of him, the brahmins and householders of Vāsava village—as previously described—sent someone to invite him for a meal.
"If it pleases you, let us go there."
Having taken up their bowls and robes, they set out on a journey toward the village of Vāsavagrāmaka. Traveling by stages on their journey, they arrived at Vāsavagrāmaka.
They were seen from afar by Senāñjaya.
He reflected:
"These people of coarse conduct have indeed arrived;
having allowed them to rest, they should be entertained with all necessary provisions."
"But they should not be sent to eat at families.
Having thus pacified them, he provided them with all necessary requisites;
however, they were not sent to eat at families.
Some among them said,
"Nanda and Upananda, we have been provided with all our requisites by this elder;
however, we have not been sent to eat at [his] families."
Others said,
"At least one thing has been accomplished: he will send messengers to the families as well."
When a junior monk arrived,
[the senior monk] had him rest, provided him with all necessary requisites, and once his fatigue from the journey was dispelled, sent him to various families for a meal.
The group of six monks became angry and said:
"Nandopananda, what kind of elder is this who acts out of favoritism and malice?
If it is because we arrived first, then we are the elders; if it is because of age, then we are the elders."
"Now, we are those who are learned;
this monk has arrived recently and is new, yet he knows our nature.
He has provided us with all these requisites and sent us to eat at the households, but not us."
He was reproached by them:
"O elder, you are such a person, driven by desire and hatred!
If they had arrived earlier, we would have acted as before," and so on, until [the end of the formula].
"Having provided him with all necessary requisites, he was sent by you to eat at the houses of the families, but we were not.
Elder, have we suffered any loss?
The group of six monks, becoming indignant, said:
But he should not remain silent; rather, he should respond to that [objection]. He was then struck down by them.
He remained silent.
Without having exhorted him or reminded him of the matter, they performed against him the formal act of suspension by force, based on his admission of the facts.
He reflected:
"Brahmins and householders are won over by suffering and alienated by comfort.
If I remain here, the brahmins and householders of Vāsavagrāma will manifest their faith;
therefore, I must depart at all times."
Having taken up his bowl and robes, he set out on a walking tour toward Śrāvastī; traveling by stages on his tour, he arrived at Śrāvastī.
He was seen by the monks and addressed by them.
Welcome, welcome, venerable Senāñjayin! We are pleased by the sight of you, but not by your arrival.
What is the reason for this?

"Having come to you, the brahmins and householders of Vāsavagrāma perform services for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; they provide refuge for those arriving from afar and those traveling toward Vāsavagrāma. Is this indeed so? "It is so."

"But as for me, the group of six monks, without having exhorted or reminded me, forcibly performed an act of suspension (*utkṣepaṇīyakarman*) against me based on a formal legal procedure (*vastukarman*).
What was the reason?
He related it exactly as it had happened.
Reproaching, reviling, and speaking out against this matter, the monks reported it to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, monks, when monks are divided, they must not perform an act of suspension by force based on a formal motion and confession, unless they have first accused and reminded the individual."
They do so;
they become guilty of an offense.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Caṇpā on the bank of the Gargā lotus pond.
At that time, the monks of the group of six performed such illegal acts as these:
namely, they acted illegally while being divided,
and they acted illegally while being united.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, monks, such illegal proceedings as these must not be carried out by the monks."
For example: when they act by means of what is not Dharma with a divided assembly, or by means of what is not Dharma with a united assembly, or by means of what is Dharma with a divided assembly,
they become guilty of an offense.
The summary verse: Not one by one, nor two, nor many;
not a group for a group; there are five who are the masters of the formal acts of the Saṃgha.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Caṃpā on the bank of the Gargā lotus pond.
At that time, the monks of the group-of-six were performing such illegal formal acts as these:
for instance, one [monk] acting alone against another.
One [monk] for two;
one for many;
and both [monks] for two.
Two [may perform] for one;
two [may perform] for many;
and many [may perform] for many.
Many [monks] for one;
many for two;
a group for a group.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, one person must not perform the ritual act for another."
Not by one person for two;
not by one person for many;
nor by two people for two.
Not by two for one;
not by two for many;
nor by many for many.
Not by many for one;
not by many for two;
not by a group for a group.
They do so;
they become guilty of an offense.
Moreover, monks, there are five who are the masters of the formal acts of the Saṃgha.
Which five?
Four monks constitute a *saṃgha*;
five monks also constitute a *saṃgha*.
Ten monks constitute a Saṃgha;
twenty monks constitute a Saṃgha, as do more than that.
There are five types of Saṃghas.
In that regard, monks, wherever four monks reside,
the Saṃgha is authorized there to perform all formal acts according to the Dharma,
with the exception of the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*) for five, the full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*) for ten, and the rehabilitation (*āvarhaṇa*) for twenty.
Wherever five [monks] reside, the Saṃgha is entitled to perform all formal acts according to the Dharma,
with the exception of the full ordination for ten and the rehabilitation for twenty.
Where ten [monks] reside,
the Saṃgha is entitled to perform all formal acts (*karmāṇi*),
with the exception of the act of *āvarhaṇa* (rehabilitation) for twenty.
Where twenty monks or more reside,
there the Saṃgha is entitled to perform all formal acts according to the Dharma. Summary verse:
A person who is to perform the duties of the fourfold assembly has been made deficient;
it is not recorded that the four types of formal acts may be performed with one who is undergoing parivāsa as the fourth member.
Monks, if four [monks] who are deficient in number perform a formal act (*karma*) that is to be carried out by a quorum of four,
it is an illegal act and an act not in accordance with the discipline;
it should not be performed in that manner.
And by that, the Saṃgha incurs an offense.
When they perform an act that requires a quorum of four with a householder as the fourth member,
that is an illegal act and an act not in accordance with the Vinaya.
And it should not be done in that manner;
by doing so, the Saṃgha would be at fault.
The same applies to a novice, a eunuch, a paṇḍaka, one who has violated a nun, a matricide, a patricide, or a murderer of an Arhat.
If those who create a schism in the Saṅgha, those who have shed the blood of a Tathāgata with a malicious mind, heretics, those who have entered the ranks of heretics,

those who live as thieves within the community, those who live separately from the community, those who do not live in the community at all, and those undergoing probation (pārivāsika)— if these four types of persons perform a formal act (karman),
it is an illegal act and an act contrary to the discipline.

And it should not be done in that manner; otherwise, the Saṃgha would be at fault. When a formal act (karma) to be performed by a group of four is carried out by four full members in accordance with the Dharma, that is a legal act (dharmakarma) and a disciplinary act (vinayakarma).
And it should be performed in this manner;
thus, the Saṃgha does not incur an offense.

A formal act (karman) to be performed by a group of four is not valid if the fourth member is a householder, nor a novice (śrāmaṇeraka), as previously stated, up to: "nor if they are performed with one who is on probation (pārivāsika) as the fourth."
That is both a legal action and a disciplinary action;
it should be carried out in this manner,
and by doing so, the Saṃgha incurs no offense.
If five persons perform a formal act (*karma*) that requires a quorum of five,
it is an illegal act (*adharmakarma*) and an act contrary to the discipline (*avinayakarma*).
It should not be done in that manner;
by doing so, the Saṃgha incurs an offense.

When a formal act (karman) that requires a quorum of five is performed with a householder as the fifth member—as previously described—up to one who is undergoing probation (pārivāsika) as the fifth member, [it is invalid].
And that is an act contrary to the Dharma and an act contrary to the Vinaya;
it should not be performed in that manner,
and the Saṃgha would thereby incur an offense of transgression.
A formal act (*karma*) that is to be performed by a group of five is carried out by a full quorum of five;
it is both a legal act (*dharmakarma*) and a disciplinary act (*vinayakarma*).
Thus should it be performed.
And by that, the Saṃgha does not commit an offense.

A formal act (*karma*) to be performed by a group of five is carried out lawfully when it is not done with a householder as the fifth, nor with a novice (*śrāmaṇeraka*), and so on as before, up to not having one who is under probation (*pārivāsika*) as the fifth;
such is a legal act and a disciplinary act (*vinaya-karma*).
And it should be performed in this manner;
thus, the Saṃgha does not incur an offense. Yet, they perform a formal act that requires a quorum of ten with fewer than ten members.
That is an illegal action and an undisciplinary action;
it should not be carried out in that manner,
and the Saṃgha would thereby incur an offense of transgression.
An action to be performed by a group of ten consists of those who have ten householders as the tenth, and so on, up to those who have ten *pārivāsika*s as the tenth;
that is an illegal action and an action contrary to the discipline,
and it should not be carried out in that manner.

And by that, the Saṃgha incurs an offense. When they perform a formal act (*karma*) that requires a group of ten with a full group of ten, it is both a legal act (*dharmakarma*) and a disciplinary act (*vinayakarma*).
And that action should be performed in this manner;

thus, the Saṃgha does not incur an offense. An action to be performed by a group of ten is done lawfully when those who have a layperson as the tenth member—as previously described—up to those who have one undergoing parivāsa as the tenth member, perform it.
That is both a legal action and a disciplinary action;
it should be carried out in this manner,
and by doing so, the Saṃgha does not incur an offense.
If they perform a formal act that requires a group of twenty with fewer than twenty members,
it is an illegal act and a non-disciplinary act;
furthermore, the Saṃgha incurs an offense through such an act.

Regarding the formal act (*karma*) to be performed by a group of twenty: if those who are householders or novices perform it, as previously described, or if those who are undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*) perform it,
that is an illegal act and an act not in accordance with the discipline.
And it should not be performed in that manner;
otherwise, the Saṃgha would be at fault.
A formal act (karman) that requires a group of twenty must be performed by a full assembly of twenty who possess the requisite qualities.
That is both a legal act and an act in accordance with the Vinaya;
it should be performed in this manner,
and by doing so, the Saṃgha incurs no offense.

An action to be performed by a group of twenty is not validly carried out if it is done by a group of twenty who are not householders, nor by novices— as previously stated— up to and including a group of twenty who are undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*).
That is a legal action (*dharmakarma*) and a disciplinary action (*vinayakarma*),
and it should be performed in this manner.
And by that [action], the Saṃgha does not incur an offense. Summary verse:
An action performed according to the Dharma or contrary to the Dharma, and that which is performed by means of a formal motion (*jñapti*).
In the presence [of the accused], by confession, by the wheel, by the peyāla, and by the saṅkalā.
Unlawful action; lawful action;
what is unlawful action?
When the time for dismissal has not yet arrived, they dismiss them before the time has come;
they do not dismiss them in the manner that the formal proclamation (*anuśrāvaṇa*) for one being dismissed takes place.
What is an illegal action? What is a legal action?
When expulsion is appropriate, they carry out the expulsion.
They carry out the removal in such a way that there is a formal proclamation for him as he is being removed;
this is a legal act (*dharmakarma*).
When the time for reinstatement has not yet arrived, they reinstate him prematurely;
they do not perform the reinstatement in the manner that the formal proclamation (*anuśrāvaṇa*) should be made for one being reinstated.
An illegal act:
when the time for reinstatement has arrived, they reinstate him;
this is according to the formal proclamation that occurs while he is being reinstated.
Likewise, they bring it up;
it is a legal act (*dharmakarma*).
They perform a formal motion (*jñapti*) without having first made the motion.
An illegal action:
they perform a formal motion (*jñapti*) after having already made the motion;
this is a legal action.
A formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*):
if they proclaim it once without having made the motion,
it is an illegal act (*adharmakarma*).
A formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation; having performed the motion, they proclaim it once.
This is a legal formal act.
A formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations; if they proclaim it three times without having made the motion,
it is an illegal formal act.
A formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations:
having made the motion, they proclaim it three times;
this is a legal formal act.

If they carry it to completion after having performed the formal motion (*jñapti*) by means of one action, it is an illegal action (*adharmakarma*). If they carry it to completion after having performed the formal motion by means of that very same action, it is [also] an illegal action.
A legal act;
they perform an act that ought to be done in the presence [of the assembly] when he is not present.
An illegal act.
They perform a formal act that requires the presence [of the accused] against one who is not present;
it is an illegal act.
They perform a formal act that requires a confession against one who does not confess.
An illegal action:
they perform an action that ought to be done by formal admission through formal admission;
this is a legal action.
To one who deserves the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence), he grants the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement based on memory).
This is an illegal act (*adharmakarma*).

[He grants] the *amūḍhavinaya* (settlement for one no longer insane), the *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* (settlement by investigation of the nature of the offense), the *yadbhūyaiṣīya* (settlement according to what has been admitted), the *pratijñākāraka* (settlement by formal admission), the *tṛṇaprastāraka* (settlement by sweeping under the carpet), and the *tarjanīya* (reprimand).

The formal act of censure (*nigarhaṇīya-karman*), the formal act of reconciliation (*pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman*), the formal act of suspension for not seeing [one's offense] (*adarśanīyotkṣepaṇīya-karman*), the formal act of suspension for not making amends (*apratikarmārhayotkṣepaṇīya-karman*), and the formal act of suspension for not relinquishing an evil view (*apratinisṛṣṭe pāpake dṛṣṭigate utkṣepaṇīya-karman*).

They impose probation (*parivāsa*), initial probation (*mūlaparivāsa*), probation with reduction from the beginning (*mūlāpakarṣaparivāsa*), penance (*mānāpya*), initial penance (*mūlamānāpya*), and penance with reduction from the beginning (*mūlāpakarṣamānāpya*); they perform the formal act of rehabilitation (*āvarhaṇa*).
An illegal action:

when one grants *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence) to one who deserves it, yet does not grant *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection), nor even up to *āvarhaṇa* (rehabilitation), this is an illegal action.
A legal action: [when one grants these in their proper order].
To one who deserves the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement based on mindfulness), he grants the *amūḍhavinaya* (settlement for one no longer insane);
this is an illegal act (*adharmakarma*).
Likewise, regarding the *yadbhūyaiṣīya* (settlement according to the majority) and so forth, as before, up until they grant the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of the accused).
An illegal action:

when one grants *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection) to one who deserves *smṛtivinaya*, yet does not grant *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* (investigation of the nature of the offense), nor anything up to *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of).
A legal action: [when one grants the appropriate settlement].
To one who deserves the *amūḍhavinaya* (the discipline for one who was not deluded),
to grant the *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* (the procedure for seeking the nature of the offense) is an illegal act.
In this way, when one grants the *yadbhūyeṣīya* up to the *saṃmukhavinaya* or the *smṛtivinaya*,

it is an illegal act (*adharmakarma*). However, when one grants the *amūḍhavinaya* to one who deserves the *amūḍhavinaya*, that is a [legitimate] *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya*, and not [one of] the *saṃmukhavinaya* or the *smṛtivinaya*.
A legal act (*dharmakarma*):
when one grants a *yadbhūyaiṣīya* (decision by majority) to one who deserves a *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* (decision according to the nature of the case), it is an illegal act (*adharmakarma*).

When one grants [any of the disciplinary measures] from the *tarjanīya* (reprimand) up to the *amūḍhavinaya* (verdict of past insanity), as previously described, to one who deserves [a specific measure], it is an illegal act.
An illegal action:

when one who is deserving of a *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* (decision by his own nature) is given only that *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya*, and not a *yadbhūyaiṣīya* (decision according to what has occurred), nor even up to an *amūḍhavinaya* (verdict of past insanity), it is an illegal action.
A legal action: [when the appropriate procedure is applied].
If they perform the act of *tarjanīya* (reprimand) against one who deserves *yadbhūyaiṣīya* (further inquiry),
it is an illegal act (*adharmakarma*).
Likewise, as before, up to the point of granting *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* (inquiry into the nature of the offense) to one who deserves *nigarhaṇīya* (censure), [it is an illegal act].
An illegal action:

when one grants a *yadbhūyeṣīya* (decision by majority) to one who deserves a *yadbhūyeṣīya*, but does not grant a *tarjanīya* (reprimand), nor anything up to a *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* (decision according to the nature of the offense).
A legal action: [when it is granted accordingly].
If they perform a formal act of censure against one who deserves a formal act of reprimand— ranging from a formal act of reconciliation up to granting a probationary period as before—
that is an illegal act. However, if they perform only the formal act of reprimand against one who deserves a formal act of reprimand, and not the remaining acts, [that is legal].
By this procedure, the summary of the wheels is as before, up to the point of "legal action" (*dharmakarma*).
When they perform an act of reconciliation (*pratisaṃharaṇīyakarman*) against one who deserves censure (*nigarhaṇīyārha*),
it is an illegal action (*adharmakarma*).
As before;
however, for one who deserves the act of censure, they perform precisely the act of censure.
This is a legal action (dharmakarma), as previously described.
If they perform an act of reconciliation against one who deserves an act of banishment,
it is an illegal act, as previously described;
however, if they perform an act of banishment against one who deserves an act of banishment, that is indeed a legal act.
A legal action (*dharmakarma*) is as previously described.
They perform an act of suspension for non-appearance against one who deserves an act of reconciliation;
this is an illegal action (*adharmakarma*), as previously described.
But for one who deserves the act of reconciliation, they perform precisely the act of reconciliation;
this is a legal act (*dharmakarma*), as previously described.
For one who deserves the act of suspension for not seeing [an offense], or for one who deserves the act of suspension for not making amends, they perform the act of suspension.
An illegal action is as previously described.
However, when they perform an act of suspension for non-seeing against one who is deserving of an act of suspension for non-seeing,
it is a legal action.
As before:
[if] one grants *parivāsa* to one who deserves the act of suspension (*utkṣepaṇīyakarman*) for being unworthy of rehabilitation (*apratikarmārha*),
it is an illegal act (*adharmakarma*), as before.
They perform a formal act of suspension (*utkṣepaṇīya-karman*) against one who has not relinquished an evil view;
this is an illegal act, as previously described.
However, against one who is fit for a formal act of suspension but is instead fit for a formal act of non-rehabilitation, they perform only the formal act of suspension.
A legal action (*dharmakarma*) is as previously described.
To one who has not renounced a wicked view and is deserving of the formal act of suspension (*utkṣepaṇīyakarman*), [the community] grants a period of probation (*parivāsa*);
this is an illegal action (*adharmakarma*), as previously described.
When one who is deserving of the *utkṣepaṇīya* (suspension) rite for not relinquishing a wicked view has indeed not relinquished that wicked view, they perform the *utkṣepaṇīya* rite against him;
this is a legal act (*dharmakarma*), as previously described.
When one who is deserving of the *parivāsa* (probation) rite is granted the *mūlaparivāsa* (initial probation).
An illegal act, as before;
however, for one who deserves the act of *parivāsa*, he grants *parivāsa* itself [instead].
An illegal act, as before.
He grants a *mūlaparivāsa* to one who deserves a *mūlaparivāsa*;
this is an illegal act (*adharmakarma*), as previously described.
However, when he grants a *mūlaparivāsa* to one who deserves a *mūlaparivāsa*, [it is legal].
A legal act is as previously described. Granting a *mānāpya* to one whose *parivāsa* has not been completed is an illegal act, as previously described.
If one grants a *mānāpya* to someone whose *parivāsa* has not been completed,
it is an illegal act (*adharmakarma*), as previously described. However, if one grants a *mānāpya* to someone whose *parivāsa* has been completed, [it is a legal act].
A legal act is as previously described.
They carry out a *mānāpya* that has not been undergone;
this is an illegal act, as previously described.

They carry out the *āvarhaṇa* for one who has completed the *mānāpya*; this is a legal act (*dharmakarma*) as previously described. They grant the *saṃmukhavinaya* to one who is subject to *āvarhaṇa*.
As before, up to the point where he grants the *mānāpya*.

It is an illegal procedure (*adharmakarma*), as before. However, for one who deserves *āvarhaṇa*, they perform only the *āvarhaṇa*; they do not grant the *saṃmukhavinaya*, nor anything up to the *mānāpya*.
A legal act (*dharmakarma*) is as previously described.
In this very same way, the detailed sequence of the wheel (*cakrapeyāla*) should be understood by a novice (*navaka*).
Summary verse (*uddāna*):
When those who are divided perform [an act] together, or when one should suspend [a monk] by means of both dharma and adharma,
these are the formal acts (karman) established according to their subject matter (vastu), including reinstatement (osāraṇā).
Dissociated action;
united action. What is dissociated action?
As many monks as have reached the boundary and reached the place of action— all of them being assembled and present, and having been brought by consent from those entitled to give their consent—
if the monks who are assembled and present oppose and protest,
and the protest of those opposing and protesting gains ground; [then that legal act is invalid].
And they perform actions;
this is called discordant action (*vyagrakarma*).
What is concordant action (*samagrakarma*)?
As many monks as have reached the boundary and reached the point of action— all of them being assembled and present, and having been brought by consent from those entitled to give their consent—
and as the monks who are assembled and present do not oppose or protest;
for those who would oppose or protest, their protest would be valid.
And they perform the ritual actions;
this is called a complete ritual action.
The Venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, for how many does a protest not take effect?

"For ten, Upāli: one who is shameless; one who has internal divisions; one who is a fool; one who is deluded; one who is unlearned; one who is unskilled; one who stands outside the boundary; one who has fallen from proper deportment; and one whose speech is unrestrained."
"To how many, O Venerable One, does a protest (pratikrośa) succeed? To four, Upāli:
one who remains in his natural state, one who stands within the boundary, one who has not deviated from his posture, and one who is restrained in speech."
The Venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, how many acts of suspension (*utkṣepaṇīya-karman*) are there?
"There are four, Upāli."
Those who are divided expel by means of what is not Dharma; those who are united [expel] by means of what is not Dharma; those who are divided [expel] by means of Dharma;
and those who are united [expel] by means of Dharma.
In that regard, there is one act of suspension (*utkṣepaṇakarman*),
namely when they suspend [a monk] in accordance with the Dharma while being in full assembly.
Venerable sir, how many acts of reinstatement (*osāraṇakarman*) are there?
There are four cases, Upāli:
they eject [a monk] through illegality while being divided; and they eject him through illegality while being united.
They are divided by means of the Dharma;
they are united by means of the Dharma.
In that regard, there is one act of reinstatement.
That which they perform in accordance with the Dharma as a united body:
the matter of the formal act is concluded.
